summary: Specifies conventions for using HTTP or HTTPS to obtain certificates and certificate revocation lists from PKI repositories. This meets some of the operational requirements of the Internet PKI. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets programs download ID badges and the list of cancelled badges with simple web requests.

questions: how to fetch certificates over http
what is a pkix certificate store
how do clients find a certificate store
subtitle: Fetch certificates and revocation lists from a PKI repository with plain HTTP GET requests.

tldr.problem: RFC 2585 only mentions fetching certificates from a static URL, which gives no general-purpose way to look certificates up in a certificate store.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends an HTTP GET whose query is one attribute and value, such as a hash of the issuer name, and the store returns the matching certificates or CRL. The RFC also defines how to find such a store via certificate extensions, DNS SRV or well-known URIs.
tldr.outcome: Any back end that can do a key and value lookup can sit behind a simple read-only HTTP interface. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 4387 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8553. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Use HTTP for Certificate Stores
sections.content:
This is one part of a multi-part standard for the Internet Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), which uses X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs). It sets out conventions for using HTTP, or optionally HTTPS, to get certificates, public keys and CRLs from PKI repositories. The RFC uses the word HTTP for both.

RFC 2585 already covers fetching certificates over HTTP, but only mentions fetching from a static URL. This document aims at a general-purpose, transparent interface to any kind of certificate or key store: flat files, databases such as Berkeley DB and relational databases, and X.500/LDAP directories.
sections.plainLanguage: Websites already know how to hand out files. This RFC uses that same skill so computers can ask for ID badges in a simple, standard way.

sections.title: The HTTP Query Interface
sections.content:
The client uses the HTTP GET method with a query URI of the form query = attribute '=' value. The attribute and value identify one or more certificates or public keys. Certificates and keys come from one URI (the certificate URI) and CRLs from another (the revocation URI); whether they are the same server is local configuration. The value MUST be form-urlencoded as in RFC 2854.

Failures use the standard HTTP handling from RFC 2616, and servers may redirect with a 3xx response. If more than one certificate matches, the answer MUST be a multipart/mixed response. Data MUST be returned verbatim, with no extra content or transfer encoding such as compression or base64, and implementations SHOULD NOT use chunked encoding.

A query MAY carry extra attribute and value pairs separated by &, and stores SHOULD ignore ones they do not recognise.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the web server with a short question like 'give me the badge with this code'. If several badges match, you get them all in one parcel, delivered exactly as they are.

sections.title: Turning Binary Data into Search Keys
sections.content:
Some fields are arbitrary-length or non-text, which makes them unsuitable for HTTP queries. Fields marked Hash are first hashed with SHA-1 to a fixed 160-bit value. Fields marked Hash or Base64 are then base64-encoded. A 20-byte value encodes to 28 bytes whose last byte is always the padding character =, which is dropped to leave a 27-byte search key. For other lengths, such as 64-bit PGP key IDs, trailing padding is simply removed.

Implementations MUST check that submitted base64 values contain only a-z, A-Z, 0-9, + and /, and MUST reject queries with any other character. Matches are exact and case sensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: Long, messy names are squashed into a short fixed-size code so they fit neatly into a web address.

sections.title: Attribute Types
sections.content:
For X.509, the attributes are certHash, uri, iHash, iAndSHash, name, sHash and sKIDHash. Certificate URIs MUST support retrieval by all of them. CRL URIs MUST support iHash and sKIDHash, which identify the CRL's issuer, and MAY support certHash and iAndSHash. A CRL query MUST return the matching CRL with the greatest thisUpdate value, meaning the most recent one.

For PGP keys the attributes are email, fingerprint, keyID and name; key URIs MUST support all of them, and revocation URIs MUST support fingerprint and keyID. For XML signatures, the same attributes apply. Applications may define their own attributes, which should begin with x- to avoid clashing with future ones.

The uri attribute is given without a scheme, so a certificate for mailto:user@example.com is looked up as user@example.com. The store returns every certificate with that URI and leaves the client to pick the best one.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a menu of ways to ask: by fingerprint of the badge, by the owner's name or email, or by who issued it. Everyone must understand the same menu.

sections.title: Design Notes and Examples
sections.content:
The informative notes explain that hashes keep long names short and show that structured name searching is not supported: this is a simple key and value store, not an HTTP front end for X.500. Servers may use only part of the 160-bit value, for example the first 40, 64, 80 or 128 bits. Certificate and CRL stores have separate URIs because a certificate store typically holds many small items while a CRL store holds few, potentially large ones.

Performance advice includes sending the HTTP header and data in a single write, to avoid a delay of about 200ms with TCP delayed ACK, and keeping headers small. The interface is read-only. Updates are left as a local configuration issue. The notes also compare it with the PGP HKP protocol, with which no compatibility is attempted.

Examples show a CA certificate lookup by sHash, a CRL lookup by iHash, and an email certificate lookup, listed in the figure below.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes explain why choices were made, such as keeping it simple and read-only, and give tips like sending the answer in one go so it is fast.

sections.title: Finding a Certificate Store
sections.content:
Relying parties can find a store in four ways. Manual configuration is the last resort.

  • In the certificate. CAs SHOULD use the SubjectInfoAccess and AuthorityInfoAccess extensions, with access methods id-ad-http-certs ({ id-ad 6 }) or id-ad-http-crls ({ id-ad 7 }), and the accessLocation is the query URI.
  • DNS SRV. The symbolic names are certificates, crls, pgpkeys and pgprevocations, for example _certificates._tcp.example.com.
  • A well-known location. Prepend the type to the domain name and append search.cgi, giving certificates.<domain_name>/search.cgi. Embedded devices with one fixed address instead use paths such as <net_loc>/certificates/search.cgi. Providers SHOULD prefer these URIs. The name does not imply CGI scripts.
  • Manual configuration of the client, which MAY also override other information.

The notes suggest an HTTP redirect from the well-known location to reach nonstandard places, or to HTTPS.
sections.plainLanguage: To find the right office, you can read the address on the badge, look it up in a directory, try the usual street name, or be told by a person.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main risk is back-end injection. If a store builds a SQL string such as SELECT certificate FROM certificates WHERE iHash = plus the search key, an attacker can supply a key like X;DELETE FROM certificates. Even read-only queries can leak data. Filtering is not enough, since a filter that removes DELETE can be bypassed. The RFC says to use parameterised queries, check both the encoded and decoded form of values, and configure the back end for read-only access, for example by opening Berkeley DB read-only or using SQL GRANT and REVOKE.

Misconfigured caching proxies may return an out-of-date certificate or CRL, even though query URLs should not be cached. Finally, the store is not a trusted directory. Fetching a key from an entity claiming to be X says nothing about its veracity, so users should verify what they fetch. HTTPS or similar protection is a local policy matter.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not let people type tricky commands into your question box, only let them read, and double-check any badge you get, because the place you got it from is not vouching for it.

data.title: Example HTTP queries
data.code:
GET /search.cgi?email=foo%40example.com HTTP/1.1
GET /search.cgi?sHash=<search key> HTTP/1.1
GET /search.cgi?sKIDHash=<search key> HTTP/1.1
GET /search.cgi?iHash=<search key> HTTP/1.1
